headlines.title: Preliminary 2.5 magnitude earthquake strikes near Gilroy
headlines.description: A preliminary 2.5 magnitude earthquake struck near Gilroy late Thursday morning, according to the United States Geological Survey. The quake hit at 10:57 a.m. and was centered 6.1 miles east-southeast of Gilroy, 9.9 miles north-northwest of Hollister and 14.5 miles southeast of Morgan Hill, the USGS said. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates. headlines.title: PG&E power shutoffs affect more than 6,000 Bay Area customers
headlines.description: PG&E had shut off power to 6,824 customers in five Bay Area counties as of Thursday morning as a safety measure ahead of forecasted high winds and dry conditions. PG&E said that as of 6 a.m., the outages affected 3,158 customers in Napa County, 2,169 in Sonoma County, 1,358 in Contra Costa County, 88 in Alameda County and 51 in Solano County. In Mendocino County, there were 444 affected customers. PG&E began shutting off power around 5:30 p.m. Wednesday as part of a Public Safety Power Shutoff. About 90,000 customers across 29 counties are included in the shutoffs, the utility said. More power shutoffs were planned for Thursday morning and Friday morning. PG&E said affected customers had received multiple notifications about the service interruptions. The utility plans to open more than 40 Community Resource Centers across 25 counties. The centers will offer device charging, Wi-Fi, bottled water, snacks and other supplies.

headlines.title: SFPD cancels remembrance event for retired Deputy Chief Ann Mannix
headlines.description: The San Francisco Police Department canceled a remembrance event honoring retired Deputy Chief Ann Mannix that was scheduled for Thursday. “We are deeply grateful for everyone’s outpouring of support during this difficult time,” the department said in a statement Wednesday night. Mannix, 65, her husband, retired Officer Kevin Mannix, 68, and their daughter, Katherine Elizabeth Mannix, 24, were found dead at their home in unincorporated Marin County on Sunday. Authorities are investigating the deaths as a suspected double-murder suicide. Kevin Mannix fatally shot his wife and daughter before shooting himself, according to the preliminary investigation by the Marin County Sheriff’s Office. Ann Mannix served with the San Francisco Police Department for more than 30 years. She worked at several district stations and in the department’s Special Operations and Field Operations bureaus. She was the first woman to lead the department’s tactical company, Police Chief Derrick Lew said. Lew previously expressed condolences to the Mannix family, friends and colleagues, saying the department was grieving and trying to process the tragedy. Mayor Daniel Lurie also praised Mannix’s decades of service to San Francisco, calling her a trailblazer who became the first woman to join and lead the department’s SWAT team.

headlines.title: Owner Joe Lacob believed in Valkyries from Day 1, but reaching WNBA Finals in second year remarkable
headlines.description: The moment Joe Lacob walks into the Chase Center and heads for his courtside seats, he and his family immediately feel the enormous energy and wholesome vibe that is the Golden State Valkyries’ “Ballhalla” home crowd game after game, sellout after violet-crazed sellout. The women’s basketball franchise Lacob always envisioned while owning the Golden State Warriors has come together in no time, and in all the right ways – from relatable players other teams overlooked to leadership from the top down and smart branding complete with a beloved raven “bestie” Violet. Just don’t dare calling her a mascot. On Saturday, Lacob will be there roaring with the rest of them as his Valkyries begin their quest for a WNBA championship in just their second year of existence. And whatever happens, he is immensely proud of the progress and the loyal support from everyone representing all walks of life who contributes to one of the best home-court advantages anywhere. “What is truly remarkable is how great our fans are. Our players love it, we love it,” Lacob said. “It’s great, it’s a cohesion, it’s everybody coming together all at the same time and rooting for something that is new and fresh and it’s timely. And people see it and feel it. What’s going on in that arena is fantastic, it’s remarkable, it’s incredibly fun. “I love walking in there, my wife, my family, we all love walking in there to the tremendous feeling of camaraderie and togetherness. We all as a team of people, fans, players, organization, together we’re making history and we all feel it.” WNBA Oct 13 WNBA Oct 12 Owner tries to back up his bold prediction For decades, Lacob has loved women’s basketball and when he brought a WNBA franchise to the Bay Area at last, the owner had no hesitations about making bold predictions. He promised a championship within the first five years. And now in the second year the Valkyries are playing for one. “I’m telling you right now, we will win a WNBA championship in the first five years of this franchise,” Lacob declared on Oct. 5, 2023, when the WNBA announced Lacob’s ownership group had been awarded an expansion franchise. “I think it just goes to show that with a new team, (you can have success) with a clear vision of what you want and the identity that you want,” center Kiah Stokes said. “Shoutout to the Valkyries organization, because they had this vision from the start, and to be able to see it come to fruition already in year two is pretty amazing and pretty special. We have a great group, it’s really special, and we’re looking forward to the finals.” Lacob had followed his prediction with the same statement to now-coach Natalie Nakase when he interviewed her to be the sideline leader. She was all in from that moment. “It’s just a perfect confluence of events and people and experience and timing. It’s just a lot of things that have all come together at the right time,” Lacob said. “I’m not going to sit here and tell you that I am shocked by this, I’m not. I think all the ingredients were there and I made that prediction knowingly and understood what I was saying, now to do it in two years, no one could sit here and tell you that would be something they would predict. No one, not even me.” Many of the Valkyries have taken unsung paths Under Lacob’s leadership and the hiring of President Jess Smith and her staff, Golden State has built a roster of understated stars. Veronica Burton got cut by Dallas two years ago, while her backup point guard Kaitlyn Chen was briefly let go by the Valkyries last season before she returned. Kayla Thornton is a 33-year-old undrafted forward out of the University of Texas El Paso who became an All-Star in 2025. Gabby Williams had something to prove in the WNBA after sensing others didn’t believe in her ability. That’s not the case anymore. “It feels special because this is a special group,” Williams said. “All we need is each other. We just need to believe in each other, we know we weren’t a team that was talked about, but just the culture and going to work every day, we felt that we had something worth fighting for. That’s how we’re going into the finals, with that same mentality — staying together and staying unselfish.” Lacob is into it, yelling from courtside in his Valkyries violet gear. But this goes back decades for him. He supported Stanford and followed along when Hall of Fame Cardinal coach Tara VanDerveer led the Americans’ gold-medal dominance at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics and Lacob became a founding owner of the San Jose Lasers in the former ABL. He is thrilled with the WNBA’s recent strides and the rise of women’s sports. NBA pros have become huge fans, too Count Warriors coach Steve Kerr as a huge fan of these Valkyries. “They’re so fun to watch, they’re so unselfish, they’re so tough, smart, well coached,” Kerr said. “And having watched this thing unfold over two years, I can’t imagine that there’s ever been a better expansion team in terms of the unveiling of everything – the brand, the colors, the name, the logo, the mascot, the vibe in the building. It’s incredible. We’re really proud of the team, excited for Natalie and her staff. We can’t wait for the finals.” It certainly helps to have Stephen Curry, Draymond Green, Brandin Podziemski and Gui Santos showing up in support. Kyrie Irving has taken notice, too. No matter who is cheering, Nakase has a message for the loyal, loud fans in a home crowd of 18,064 — including her top boss, Lacob — she is so counting on bringing their support to another level. “Since we’re prepping for a great game plan, Ballhalla better be prepping for a game plan,” Nakase said. “So as soon as they’re announced, I need some hostility. If they do a challenge, I need hostility, and if they’re shooting free throws, I need that thing to be rocking. Game plan, Ballhalla, get ready, get prepped.” ___ See AP’s full WNBA coverage here

headlines.title: Black Panther Party stalwarts to celebrate 1966 founding in Oakland, programs that aided the poor
headlines.description: The legacy of the Black Panther Party lives on six decades after its founding, in the work of a Seattle medical center started to address systemic health disparities in the African American community, particularly among Black children. Originally known as the Sidney Miller Free Medical Clinic in 1969, it put into practice the national Black Panther Party’s Ten-Point Program to uplift African Americans as the Black Power movement gained momentum. Now, as the Carolyn Downs Family Medical Center, it, along with the affiliated Country Doctor Community Clinic, sees tens of thousands of patients in a year. As the celebration begins Thursday for the Black Panther Party’s Oct. 15, 1966, founding in Oakland, California, former members are looking beyond the iconic black leather jackets, berets and clenched fists to highlight programs aimed at healing disenfranchised and forgotten communities. From free medical clinics and pushing nationally for sickle cell anemia testing to providing free breakfasts for children and community schools promoting education and literacy, the Black Panthers understood what was needed during the racially turbulent 1960s, said Fredrika Newton, widow of co-founder Huey P. Newton. “We sought to meet the basic needs of the Black community, not only the Black, but all oppressed communities,” she told The Associated Press Tuesday. “Children were going to school hungry. People couldn’t get medical care. People were sleeping in the streets, just like today.” A planned four-day conference this weekend in downtown Oakland includes a gala. Surviving original members and other Black Panther Party veterans are expected to attend. Pushing for Black empowerment and against racist policing Co-founders Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale were students at Merritt College in Oakland, where they formed the Panthers during the Civil Rights Movement. Both became active in Bay Area politics during the mid-1960s and believed the Civil Rights movement may have addressed the plight of Blacks in Southern states, but it failed to bring about any real change in the U.S. West and North. With Newton as minister of defense and Seale as the group’s chair, the Black Panther Party for Self-Defense advocated for political and economic empowerment and initiatives to improve life for the city’s Black residents in addition to standing up to what they saw as racist and heavy-handed policing in the Black community. “We knew that Black people were getting brutalized by the police,” said Fredrika Newton, who joined the Black Panther Party in 1971 after meeting Huey P. Newton. “We wanted to make sure that they were getting educated and taught how to protect themselves.” Confrontations with law enforcement — broadcast to households across the country — galvanized Black support for the organization but also worried many white people. Seale, declaring that the Second Amendment right to bear arms also applied to Blacks, led a small group of armed Panthers in 1967 into the California state legislature. The Black Panther Party was targeted by the FBI, which put its leaders and members under surveillance and operated a yearslong disruption and discrediting campaign. John “Bunchy” Crear was caught up in the maelstrom of race and politics sweeping across California in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Crear, along with some friends, began attending Black Panther political education classes in 1970. He joined at age 19. “I was at home in my bedroom listening to my music when my mother comes in and says two white gentlemen from the FBI were in the living room wanting to talk to me,” recalled Crear, 74, who lives in Houston. “I walked in and there were the men in black. They asked if I was a member of the Black Panther Party, then pulled a book out with photos asking if I knew this person, if I knew that person.” “’Well, John, if you stay in school and get you a good job, you’ll never hear from us again,’” Crear said the men told him before leaving. Healthcare part of community survival programs The Black Panther Party purchased buildings and homes that served as safe houses and centers for their community survival programs, which mostly addressed food insecurity, lack of healthcare, unequal education and other issues in Black communities. Chapters were started in about 70 other cities. The chapter in Seattle started one of the 13 original Black Panther Party-founded healthcare clinics across the country and is the only one still in operation. “Thinking especially about Black folks in the 1960s and 70s, it was impossible to try to address one need and not all because they were vulnerable and under threat in so many areas,” said Brandy Taylor, chief executive of the Carolyn Downs Family Medical Center and Country Doctor Community Clinic. “It wasn’t just about medical care. It was about free speech, social services, food security and knowing your rights. There were so many doors closed that you couldn’t survive without addressing them all,” she said. From the end to emulation The Black Panther Party folded in 1982 after years of police surveillance, as well as dwindling national membership, infighting, allegations of embezzlement and scandals in which Huey P. Newton was implicated and criminally charged. Newton’s addictions to alcohol and drugs overtook him. He was murdered in Oakland, California, in 1989 by a drug dealer. In 2021, a bronze bust of Huey P. Newton was unveiled in Oakland. However, some see similarities in why the Black Panthers were started with the emergence of the Black Lives Matter movement following the 2013 acquittal of the man who killed Trayvon Martin, a Black teenager in Sanford, Florida. “We want to let young people know exactly what we did and what could be done,” said Fredrika Newton, who also is president and co-founder of the Huey P. Newton Foundation. “This is not a blueprint for what they can do now, but they can certainly see what we did, take what we did, apply them to the conditions today and organize,” she said. “Organize around the needs that exist today.” _____________ Williams is a Detroit-based member of AP’s Race & Ethnicity team.

headlines.title: Pet emu runs loose in Santa Cruz before being corralled
headlines.description: Authorities in Santa Cruz recently responded to an unusual call of an emu running in and out of traffic. The California Highway Patrol said it received several calls about the giant bird running into traffic near Harper Street and 17th Avenue. “While we often deal with dogs, cats, deer, and occasionally birds, an Emu was unexpected!” CHP Santa Cruz said in a social media post. The CHP said the emu’s owner quickly came out and was able to corral their feathery pet.

headlines.title: Man killed in scooter crash during San Francisco police chase identified
headlines.description: A man who died on Monday after crashing a scooter in San Francisco’s South of Market neighborhood while being chased by police was identified Wednesday as 56-year-old Edwin Michael Adams. Adams was a resident of Contra Costa County, according to the San Francisco Medical Examiner’s Office. He died at a hospital after suffering severe injuries when he crashed into a pole at a bus stop at Eighth and Mission streets while allegedly fleeing from police officers who were in pursuit, according to a statement from the San Francisco Police Department. A spokesperson for the police department said Adams was wanted on an arrest warrant but declined to say what that warrant was for. The investigation was ongoing, the police department’s spokesperson said.

headlines.title: 4 arrested in shooting of 49ers player Keion White at San Francisco nightclub
headlines.description: Four suspects have been arrested in connection with the February shooting of San Francisco 49ers player Keion White at a Mission District nightclub, San Francisco officials announced Wednesday. The arrests were made in various cities across California and Georgia following a monthslong investigation that included more than 50 search warrants and assistance from over 250 law enforcement personnel, officials said. White, a defensive lineman for the 49ers, was shot in the early morning hours of Feb. 9 at the Dahlia nightclub, where he was hosting an event after the Super Bowl. “It started when multiple suspects, some brandishing firearms, confronted the 49ers player, which then led to a physical altercation between the group and the victim, who was shot in the leg,” San Francisco police Chief Derrick Lew said. White has since recovered following surgery and has been playing for the 49ers this season. Keion White May 2 Ricky Pearsall Sep 19, 2025 Following several months of investigation, officers last week served four no-bail arrest warrants. Atlanta police arrested 38-year-old Marquis Davis at his home last Wednesday. Officers found an illegal firearm, 820 grams of MDMA, 1,026 grams of methamphetamine, 979 grams of cocaine and 3,842 grams of fentanyl, police said. That same morning, San Francisco police and San Joaquin County sheriff’s deputies arrested 36-year-old Antoine Washington in Stockton. Officers recovered a loaded firearm, more than 120 oxycodone pills and roughly $7,000, according to police. In Southern California on the same day, San Francisco police and Irvine police took 35-year-old Curtis Green into custody without incident. The fourth suspect and alleged shooter, 36-year-old Gregory Walker of Mountain House, was arrested last Friday in Los Angeles, police said. “We will not tolerate any type of violence in our city, but certainly not gun violence,” San Francisco District Attorney Brooke Jenkins said. “We had a great, amazing Super Bowl weekend that ended with this incident. I am just so thankful to the San Francisco police that we are being able to hold those accountable who sadly chose violence on that night.” Walker has since been charged with assault with a firearm with allegations that he personally discharged that firearm at White, Jenkins said. Walker also was charged with possession of a firearm by a felon, possession of a concealed firearm by a felon and possession of a loaded firearm by a felon. Jenkins said the district attorney’s office filed a motion to keep Walker in custody because they believe he poses a public safety risk. A judge agreed during Walker’s first court appearance Wednesday, ordering him to be held without bail for the time being and pushing his formal arraignment to Monday. Walker’s attorney, Jeff Wozniak, said even though Walker was arrested in Los Angeles, he lives in San Francisco and did not do what he’s accused of. “Mr. Walker is a family man, a longshoreman, a union member,” Wozniak said. “We’re going to show that he’s innocent and get him back to his family.” Green faces multiple misdemeanors, including brandishing a firearm and carrying a concealed weapon, Jenkins said. In court, he was ordered to be released from custody. San Francisco police are working with the district attorney’s office and prosecutors in other jurisdictions to arrange for Davis and Washington to be transferred to the city to face charges, Lew said. The February shooting marked the second time in two years that a 49ers player was shot in the city. Wide receiver Ricky Pearsall was shot and injured during an alleged attempted robbery in Union Square in August 2024. He made a full recovery. NBC News contributed to this report.

headlines.title: 1 injured in fire in SF's Cathedral Hill neighborhood
headlines.description: A person was injured in a one-alarm fire early Thursday morning in San Francisco’s Cathedral Hill neighborhood, according to fire officials. The fire was reported at 2:54 a.m. in the 1600 block of Gough Street, at the intersection of Bush and Austin streets, the San Francisco Fire Department said on social media. Crews contained the blaze at 3:15 a.m. The injured person was sent to a local hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. No one was reported displaced. Meanwhile, crews also contained a fire on the 5th floor of a building in the 900 block of Howard Street in South of Market neighborhood. The department said it started at 1:12 a.m. and was contained just before 1:30 a.m. No injuries or displacements were reported in the blaze. Both fires are under further investigation.

headlines.title: San Jose high school athletic trainer accused of sexual battery
headlines.description: A high school athletic trainer was accused of sexual battery and owning child sexual abuse material (CSAM), San Jose police said on Wednesday. Police said they responded to a report of sexual battery at Archbishop Mitty High School on Oct. 8 around 7:30 p.m. There, officers contacted a 16-year-old female student, who said a man was providing care for her sports-related injury when he sexually battered her and recorded it on his phone, authorities said. Officials said the suspect was identified as 31-year-old Kelvin Chiu, an athletic trainer for the school. Detectives obtained a search warrant for the suspect, his home and vehicles, according to the police department. Authorities said Chiu was located and apprehended in Fremont on Oct. 9. After serving a search warrant at his home, detectives found CSAM on Chiu’s phone, the police department said. The suspect was transported and booked into the Santa Clara County Main Jail in connection to crimes related to annoying or molesting a minor, production and possession of CSAM, and sexual battery, according to authorities. Cynthia Shaw, the director of communications for the Diocese of San Jose, said Chiu has been an employee of Archbishop Mitty High School since May 2025. Shaw said Chiu was placed on administrative leave. Due to Chiu’s position of trust, the police department said there may be additional victims. They encourage anyone with information about these cases to contact Detective Camarillo and Detective Widmer of the San Jose Police Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC)/Child Exploitation Detail (CED) Task Force via email: 4576@sanjoseca.gov, and 4581@sanjoseca.gov or by calling 408-277-4102. Shaw’s statement reads, in part: “Our first concern is for the student and family, and for all of our students and families. We recognize the impact a situation of this nature may have on our students, and the school’s Counseling teams will be available to speak with students who may need additional support. “We encourage any victim-survivor to come forward and report incidents of improper conduct either historically or currently occurring at any diocesan parish, school or ministry. To report any other concerns, we encourage individuals to first contact their local civil authorities (law enforcement). Once a report is filed with the local civil authorities, individuals are encouraged to contact the diocesan Office for the Protection of Children & Vulnerable Adults at (408) 983-0113. All reports are confidential to protect the rights of the victim. Reports to the Diocese are accepted by either online submission or by phone. For online submission, please use the following URL to access our secure third-party reporting server designated for this purpose: https://opcva.ethicspoint.com or contact our toll-free 24-hour reporting hotline at 844-372-1691.”

headlines.title: Chevron refinery in Richmond issues alert on flaring activity
headlines.description: Chevron issued an alert for people who live near its refinery in Richmond due to flaring activity at the facility. Chevron says the public does not need to evacuate or take any action. It says flares are highly regulated safety devices used to relieve pressure during the refining process. Officials say it also helps keep their equipment operating safely. Chevron says a team is working quickly to stop the flaring.

headlines.title: California sues to block planned closure of National Archives at San Francisco
headlines.description: California Attorney General Rob Bonta is taking the Trump administration to court in hopes of blocking the planned closure of the San Francisco National Archives facility in San Bruno. Bonta said the closure would scatter more than 175 years of historical records across the country, creating new challenges for the families, researchers and tribal communities that rely on them. “We are here to protect generations of California history,” Bonta said Wednesday. “Records that belong to the people of this state need to remain here to be accessible to the people of this state.” The federal government has said the San Francisco National Archives collection would be spread out among five National Archives facilities across the country and the San Bruno facility would be closed to cut costs. Bonta argues the government failed to properly consider the impact or give the public a meaningful opportunity to weigh in. “[The National Archives and Records Administration] did none of that,” Bonta said. “Instead, it decided unilaterally and behind closed doors to pack up our history and ship it away.” The Trump administration did not immediately comment on the lawsuit. NBC Bay Area’s Ali Reid has more in the video report above. San Bruno Aug 24 San Bruno Aug 20 New effort underway to save National Archives sites, including one in San Bruno
